1310.title: The thousand years (Revelation 20)
1310.hook: Christians read the millennium as literal, symbolic, or as the church age now
1310.tomorrow: A new heaven and a new earth
1310.howItsDone: Churches and Christian teachers differ on the thousand years: some teach a future reign of Christ on earth, some a long age of peace before his return, and some read it as the present age of the church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the marriage supper of the Lamb, and a bride in linen given to her. Your line was the wedding feast.

Three friends at a church potluck, paper plates in hand, get onto Revelation twenty. One says the thousand years are coming: Christ will return and reign on earth, a real, long age of peace. The second says the gospel will slowly fill the world, and the long peace comes first, before he returns. The third says it's happening already: the thousand years is a picture of now, the time of the church, with Christ reigning from heaven. All three have read the same chapter, and all three take it seriously. And they go back for seconds together.

Millennium means a thousand years, and the thousand years is this chapter's phrase. First, the text. An angel lays hold on "the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years." The faithful "lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years." Then the dragon is let loose for a little while, and finally defeated. Second, the three readings. Some Christians, called premillennial, read a future reign of Christ on earth after he returns. Some, called postmillennial, expect a long age of peace as the gospel spreads, and then his return. And some, called amillennial, read the thousand years as symbolic: the present age of the church, with Christ reigning now. Augustine, in The City of God, read it that way. Each reading has faithful Christians behind it, and churches have held them side by side. Third, a hint from another letter. Second Peter says: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." Some readers take that as a caution against reading the number like a calendar. Fourth, what all three share. However they read the thousand years, the chapter ends the same way: books are opened, the dead are judged by what they did, and "death and hell were cast into the lake of fire." Death itself is thrown away. The friends argue over details; all three still say he reigns.

Bring to mind a question about faith or life you don't have settled, maybe this one, maybe something closer to home. Rest your hands open in your lap, as if holding it there: you don't have to drop it, and you don't have to grip it. If you pray, hold it up to God and say you'll trust what you can't yet see; if not, just breathe with an open hand.
Millennium. A thousand years, from Revelation twenty, read by Christians as a future reign, a coming age of peace, or the age of the church now.
Your line: he reigns. Three readings of the thousand years, and one ending. Go gently.

1311.title: A new heaven and a new earth (Revelation 21:1–4)
1311.word: A new heaven and a new earth
1311.hook: God will dwell with them; no more death, mourning, crying or pain
1311.howItsDone: Revelation 21:1–4 is read at Christian funerals and memorial services, and Christians speak of it as the hope behind visiting the sick, comforting the grieving and caring for the earth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the thousand years, read three ways, and death itself thrown away at the end. Your line was he reigns.

Which way does heaven move? One familiar picture points up: when it's all over, people go up there. Revelation twenty-one points the other way. John sees the new Jerusalem, and it isn't waiting above the clouds for anyone to climb to. It's coming down: "And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband." After the beasts, the fallen city and the thousand years, the closing vision of the Bible isn't people leaving earth. It's heaven arriving.

First, the opening line: "And I saw a new heaven and a new earth: for the first heaven and the first earth were passed away; and there was no more sea." Isaiah had heard God promise it: "For, behold, I create new heavens and a new earth." John sees it happen. And no more sea. In chapter thirteen, the beast rose from the sea. Some readers hear its absence as the end of chaos and danger; others as the end of distance, nothing left to divide people. Second, God moves in: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God." Tabernacle is the old word for a tent, like the one Israel carried through the desert for God's presence. At the end, God pitches the tent among people. Third, what's gone: "And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away." Not new things added; old things missing. No funerals. No hospitals. No crying in the car before you go inside. Fourth, now. Christians who read it this way say it isn't only a picture of later. It's the shape they hope toward, and some say it's why they visit the sick and sit with the grieving today: practicing a world where God lives next door.
screen: `A NEW HEAVEN, AND NO MORE SEA.`

segments.voice: Picture one place where people cry, a hospital waiting room, a courthouse hallway, a kitchen after bad news, and let it slowly change: the chairs empty, no one waiting for a call, no one hiding red eyes. Stay with that for a few breaths; if you pray, say Revelation twenty-one, verse four, slowly, and if not, let the picture rest. Then ask what one small thing would make that room a little more like it.
A new heaven and a new earth. John's vision in Revelation twenty-one: the old order passed away, God dwelling with people, and death and crying gone.

1312.title: All things new (Revelation 21:5–8)
1312.hook: behold, I make all things new
1312.howItsDone: Some churches read Revelation 21 at funerals, and Christians also hear its 'all things new' alongside Paul's words about becoming a new creature in Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new heaven and a new earth, and God dwelling with people. Your line was no more tears.

A chipped bowl, glued back together, the crack still showing. A coat with a patch on the elbow. A friendship that broke and then, slowly, didn't. Mending doesn't swap one thing for another. It's the same thing, made whole. John has just seen a new heaven and a new earth, and a holy city coming down. Now the one on the throne speaks, and the King James gives the words like this: "Behold, I make all things new." Listen to the order. Not all new things. All things, new.
screen: `NOT ALL NEW THINGS. ALL THINGS, NEW.`

segments.voice: First, the sentence: "And he that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new." Some readers lean on the wording: the old world isn't thrown out while a fresh one is unpacked; the things themselves are made new. Others hear a cleaner break, since verse one says the first heaven and the first earth "were passed away." Christians hold both readings, and the chapter holds both lines. Second, the tense. The King James says I make, not I will make. Some readers hear it already under way, not only at the end. Paul writes something close to Corinth: "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." Third, the next breath. John is told, "Write: for these words are true and faithful." Then: "It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end." The one who started the story finishes it. And a gift: "I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely." Freely. Thirst is all the verse asks for. Fourth, the hard edge. Verse eight names the fearful, the unbelieving, murderers, liars and others, and gives them their part in the lake of fire. Christians read it more than one way: a real judgment, a warning meant to turn people around, or a picture of what can't live in a world made whole. The passage keeps the promise and the warning side by side.

Choose one small thing within reach: a smudged glass, a crooked picture, a message gone stale on your phone. Hold it in your mind and see it made fresh, clean, straight, answered, and notice that it's still itself. If you pray, hold the words "Behold, I make all things new" in the quiet; if not, just breathe with the one thing you chose.
All things new. The promise from the throne in Revelation twenty-one, heard by some readers as the same things made whole, and by others as a fresh start after the old has passed away.
Your line: all things new. Spoken by the one who started the story. That's today, done.

1313.title: The city with open gates (Revelation 21:9–27)
1313.hook: the gates are never shut, and the nations bring their glory in
1313.howItsDone: The phrase 'pearly gates' comes from the gates of pearl in Revelation 21:21, and some churches read the vision of the holy city at funerals and on feasts of dedication.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the one on the throne said, behold, I make all things new. Your line was all things new.

What's a city wall for? Keeping danger out, and people safe after dark. When Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, he ordered that the gates not open until the sun was hot, and that the doors be shut and barred. In today's passage an angel carries John to a great high mountain and shows him the holy Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven. It has a wall, great and high, and twelve gates, each a single pearl. If you've heard of the pearly gates, here they are. And then one line turns the whole idea of a city wall inside out.

First, the names. On the twelve gates are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel; on the wall's twelve foundations, the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The city carries both. Second, what's missing: "And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it." No need of sun or moon either: God's glory lights it, and the Lamb is its light. No special holy building, because the whole place is near to God. Third, the gates: "And the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there." Never shut by day, in a city with no night: never shut. And look who walks in: "And they shall bring the glory and honour of the nations into it." The kings of the earth come carrying their glory. Two chapters earlier, they gathered to make war against the rider on the white horse. Now they arrive at an open gate. Isaiah had pictured something like it: Jerusalem's gates open continually, not shut day nor night, with the wealth of the nations brought in. Fourth, the edge. Verse twenty-seven says nothing that defiles will enter, only those written in the Lamb's book of life. Christians read the open gates and that verse differently. Some hear a welcome that reaches very wide; others, an open city with a clear standard. The chapter sets them side by side and lets both stand.
screen: `NO TEMPLE, NO NEED OF THE SUN.`

The city with open gates. Revelation's holy Jerusalem: twelve gates of pearl, no temple, no night, and gates that are never shut.

1314.title: Leaves for healing (Revelation 22:1–5)
1314.hook: a river of life, and a tree whose leaves heal the nations
1314.howItsDone: Some Christians read Revelation 22 alongside Genesis 2–3 as the Bible's last garden answering its first, and some churches read 'the healing of the nations' at services of prayer for peace.

segments.voice: Yesterday, twelve pearl gates, no temple, no night. Your line was the gates are never shut.

The Bible's first garden has a tree of life in the middle. The last time Genesis shows that tree, there's a guard in front of it: God placed "Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life." The garden is left behind, and the story moves on. Now turn to the Bible's last chapter. An angel shows John a river, clear as crystal, running from the throne down the middle of the city's street. On either side of it stands the tree of life. No cherubim. No sword. And its leaves have a job.

First, the river: "a pure river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb." Ezekiel once saw a river flowing from the temple, deepening as it went, with trees on its banks whose fruit was for food and whose leaf was for medicine. Revelation sets that picture in the holy city. Second, the tree "bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit every month." Never out of season; no month when the branches are bare. Third, the leaves: "and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations." Not one people. The nations. Earlier in this book, "the nations were angry." Here they're being healed. And healing means there were wounds. Readers have asked why a city with no more pain still needs leaves for healing. Some hear healing that has already done its work; others, the long mending of old wounds between peoples, still going on in the city's light. The text doesn't settle it. Fourth, what's gone and what's given: "And there shall be no more curse." Some readers hear the curse after the first garden lifted here. Then a line to set beside Moses, who was told no one could see God's face and live: "And they shall see his face." The way to the tree is open again, and the face is no longer hidden.
screen: `NO MORE CURSE. THEY SEE HIS FACE.`

segments.voice: Touch a leaf if one's near, a houseplant, a tree, a sprig of herbs, or a leaf in a picture, and notice its veins, its edges, how it feeds a whole plant by taking in light. Then think of one wound between people you know, two relatives, two neighbors, two sides of a group chat, and without fixing it, hold the leaf and hold them. If you pray, bring them by name; if not, just breathe with the leaf in your hand.
Leaves for healing. The tree of life by the river in Revelation twenty-two, bearing fruit every month, its leaves for the healing of the nations.
Your line: the healing of the nations. Even the nations that were angry. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1315.title: Come, Lord Jesus (Revelation 22:6–21)
1315.hook: the Bible ends with a prayer: even so, come, Lord Jesus
1315.howItsDone: Some Christians say 'come, Lord Jesus' in a grace before meals, and some churches sing or pray maranatha during Advent, the weeks of waiting before Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tree of life by the river, its leaves for the healing of the nations. Your line was the healing of the nations.

Two voices, one after the other, in the second-to-last verse of a Christian Bible. The one who testifies to these things says, "Surely I come quickly." And the answer comes straight back: "Amen. Even so, come, Lord Jesus." Then one line of blessing, and the book is closed. After a garden, a flood, kings and exile, a cross and an empty tomb, beasts and a city of gold, the answer near the very end is one short word: come. Today's word is an even older way of saying it, in a language that isn't Greek at all.

First, the word. In the King James, maranatha turns up near the end of Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, left untranslated, in a hard line: "let him be Anathema Maranatha." Paul writes in Greek, but this word is Aramaic, and he doesn't explain it, as if the church already knew it. Readers divide it two ways. Marana tha: our Lord, come. Or maran atha: our Lord has come. A plea or a statement; the letters can carry both. Revelation's ending echoes the plea. Second, everyone is saying it: "And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come." The same word goes up to Christ and out to anyone thirsty. Third, quickly. Christians have read it as soon in time, sudden when it happens, or simply certain. The book doesn't explain, and the church has kept saying come anyway. Fourth, where the word lives now. Paul tells the Corinthians that when they eat the bread and drink the cup, they "shew the Lord's death till he come." So the waiting is kept at a table. Some Christians say "come, Lord Jesus" in a grace before meals. Some churches sing maranatha in Advent, the weeks before Christmas. And the very last verse of the Bible isn't a warning at all: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen."
screen: `THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY COME.`
`KEPT AT A TABLE, ENDED IN GRACE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, let the old word ride on your breath in four even, unhurried syllables, ma-ra-na-tha, the way some Christian meditation groups say it, coming back to it whenever your mind wanders. If you don't pray, sit with the plain English word come, and notice what you're waiting for: someone to arrive, something to mend, an ending to be good. Either way, don't hurry it.
Maranatha. An Aramaic word Paul left untranslated: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. At the end of Revelation: even so, come, Lord Jesus.

1316.title: Rapture and return
1316.hook: some Protestants expect believers to be caught up before tribulation; other Christians read 1 Thessalonians 4 differently
1316.howItsDone: Some Protestant churches teach a rapture of believers before a time of tribulation; the Catholic and Orthodox churches and other Protestants read 1 Thessalonians 4 as part of Christ's one return, and some churches read the passage at funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bible's near-last words, and an old Aramaic one: maranatha. Your line was come, Lord Jesus.

A bumper sticker warns that the car may suddenly be driverless. Novels and films show people vanishing mid-sentence, clothes left in a heap on the seat. Some Christians call that coming moment the rapture; other Christians grew up in churches where it was never taught. It came up briefly back on day two hundred sixteen, on the Mount of Olives. Both groups read the same short passage, a few lines near the end of Paul's first letter to the church in Thessalonica.

First, why Paul wrote it. Not to give a timetable. Some in the young church had died, and the living were grieving and afraid: "I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope." It begins as a letter to people at a graveside. Second, the picture: "For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first: Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air." The word rapture isn't in the King James text. It says caught up. Third, the readings. Some Protestants, many of them dispensationalists, read a gathering of believers before a time of great tribulation, with Christ's visible return later. Other Christians, among them the Catholic and Orthodox churches and other Protestants, read it as part of Christ's one return at the end: the dead raised, the living gathered up to meet him. Some readers hear in meet a town going out to greet an arriving guest and walk him back in: a welcome party. Fourth, the lines Paul ends on: "and so shall we ever be with the Lord. Wherefore comfort one another with these words." Whatever the timetable, Paul ends with together, and with comfort.

Read 1 Thessalonians four, verses thirteen to eighteen, slowly, out loud if you can, and let one phrase stay: "comfort one another with these words." Bring to mind someone who is grieving, or someone you've lost; there's no question about the end to settle, only the people the letter was written for. If you pray, hold them before God; if not, hold them in mind. And if grief feels too heavy to carry alone, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Rapture. A name, not in the King James text, for being caught up to meet the Lord in the air. Christians read the passage in more than one way.
Your line: ever with the Lord. From all things new to come, Lord Jesus, this week ended in comfort. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: My church never taught the rapture. Did we miss something everyone believes?
options: Churches differ: some read Paul as a gathering before a tribulation, others as part of Christ's one return.
Yes, every church has always taught it the same way, so your church simply left it out by mistake.
No, the idea comes only from Revelation; Paul never wrote a word about being caught up.
